title: Layan should have grown older
subtitle: Literary essay | Page, Screen & Power. In AlRawabi School for Girls, Haya Zaatry’s “Borders & Promises” becomes a farewell to a girl killed by her brother. Beyond the screen, the question is how families and institutions turn a girl’s freedom into something punishable—and what it would take to protect her.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: Contains spoilers for both seasons and discussion of gender-based killing.

At Layan’s memorial, Rania sings for someone who can no longer answer. Her performance of Palestinian musician Haya Zaatry’s “Borders & Promises” gives AlRawabi School for Girls a different kind of ending: the girl who once occupied so much space in other people’s lives is now an absence they must live around.

The first season closes with a gunshot after Layan’s brother Hazem finds her with her boyfriend. The second season confirms her death. What had briefly remained a question for viewers becomes a permanent fact for the characters.
But a memorial should do more than settle a plot.

Layan should have grown older. She should have had time to reconsider herself, repair the harm she caused and become someone her schoolmates could not yet imagine. The life taken from her includes all the versions of herself she never had the chance to meet.
A girl does not have to be innocent to deserve to live
Layan is a bully. That is essential to the moral difficulty of remembering her.

The series initially places viewers beside the girls she hurts. Their anger is understandable; their wish for consequences is not itself monstrous. Yet the revenge plot unfolds in a world where exposing a girl’s private life can do far more than embarrass her. Other people already possess the power to punish her for it.

The distinction is between accountability and annihilation. Layan can be responsible for cruelty without forfeiting her right to safety. Her brother’s decision to kill her does not become less his responsibility because another girl made her whereabouts known.

This is where the phrase “honour killing” needs to be held at a distance. It describes the justification claimed for a killing, not a quality the act possesses. Letting “honour” stand unchallenged risks organising the story around the perpetrator’s injured standing rather than the person whose life he took.

To mourn Layan honestly is to refuse a familiar bargain: that a dead girl must first be made obedient, modest or faultless before she can be defended. She deserved to live as the complicated girl she was.
What the song carries into the room

“Borders & Promises” was not written as Layan’s elegy. In a 2022 interview with +972 Magazine, Zaatry discussed the political borders that divide lives across the Levant; the publication described the song through lovers separated by those borders.
That Palestinian context matters. It should not disappear merely because a television drama gives the song another emotional setting.

At the memorial, however, separation acquires another meaning. A song associated with distance between living people accompanies a distance that cannot be crossed. Read through Layan’s story, its title also opens a question about the boundaries placed around a girl’s life: where she may go, whom she may love, and who claims the authority to decide.

This is an interpretation of the song’s use in the drama, not a claim that Zaatry wrote it about family violence. Its force lies in what the juxtaposition makes us hear: longing beside a future that has been deliberately closed.
The architecture of control
The gunshot is the most visible act. It is not the only place to look.

The system worth examining begins when a family treats a girl’s choices as collective property. A relationship becomes a public offence; a rumour becomes grounds for surveillance; disobedience becomes a threat to someone else’s authority. The danger deepens when institutions accept that account of the problem.

In Jordan, where AlRawabi is set, Amnesty International’s 2019 investigation documented women detained after leaving home without male relatives’ permission or being accused of relationships outside marriage. Its research involved 121 interviews, including meetings with officials. It was an investigation of practices and experiences, not a representative survey of Jordanian women.

The government disputed that women were imprisoned solely for being absent from home. Interior Ministry officials also told Amnesty that detention could protect women from relatives who might kill them. Amnesty acknowledged the opening of the Dar Amneh shelter as an important reform, while reporting that detention continued.
The contradiction remains stark: if the person threatened loses her freedom while the threat governs the terms of her release, protection can reproduce the authority she needs protection from.

This is not merely a historical concern. Human Rights Watch’s World Report 2026, covering events in 2025, reported continuing detention of women following male guardians’ complaints. That finding does not establish how many girls face lethal danger today. It does show why scrutiny must extend beyond individual perpetrators to the public powers that can reinforce family control.

Nor is such scrutiny an indictment of an entire society. Jordanian women’s organisations have fought these practices for years. They belong at the centre of this story as people challenging the system, not as footnotes to a portrait of supposedly unchanging “culture.”
What we can count—and what we cannot

There is no sufficiently reliable, current worldwide count of “honour” killings in the evidence reviewed for this piece. Different definitions, incomplete recording and concealed motives make a neat global total misleading.
There are, however, documented measures of the wider violence.

UN Women and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime estimated that around 50,000 women and girls were killed by intimate partners or other family members worldwide in 2024—approximately 137 each day. Those are estimates of partner and family killings, not a count of “honour” killings, and they do not tell us how many victims were school-age girls.

In Pakistan, the independent Human Rights Commission reported at least 405 “honour” killings in its account of 2024, released in April 2025. That reported minimum should not be presented as a complete census or as 405 girl victims: the release does not provide that age-and-sex breakdown.

In England and Wales, police recorded 2,949 “honour-based” abuse offences in the year ending March 2025. Twenty-two per cent involved controlling or coercive behaviour. These figures cover offences, not a tally of murdered women, and not necessarily distinct victims.

The Home Office explicitly warns that police records capture only part of the abuse and cannot reliably establish its prevalence or trend. A rise in recorded offences can partly reflect better identification and recording.
These measures cannot be added together. What they do establish is that the problem extends beyond a television setting—and beyond the moment when violence becomes fatal.
A memorial is not a safeguarding system
The institutional question is what happens when a girl speaks while she is still alive.

Does a school hear a safety concern or a disciplinary problem? Does a professional assume that informing her family will protect her? Is there somewhere she can go without surrendering her education, privacy and future?

British government guidance on forced marriage explicitly warns against initiating family mediation or reconciliation, noting that people have been murdered during mediation. It also warns schools that approaching relatives can expose a student to greater danger. The lesson is specific: family involvement cannot automatically be treated as a safeguard when family members may be the source of the threat.

Protection requires trained assessment, safe accommodation, confidential routes to help and accountability for those making threats. It must offer more than instructions to behave differently. A girl cannot be made responsible for preventing another person’s violence by becoming perfectly compliant.
Rania’s song can hold grief. It cannot give Layan back the years she should have had.

The responsibility beyond the screen is to build a world in which a frightened girl can be heard before she becomes someone people gather to remember. The living do not need a better memorial. They need somewhere safe to grow older.
The Athena Perspective.
